characters.name_or_role: wife (claymation woman, bun hairstyle, brown sweater)
personality_traits: emotionally expressive and quick to voice dissatisfaction ('We don't have anything in common anymore')
fidgety/anxious under the surface, hands stay clasped in her lap through the whole scene
reactive rather than proactive in the exchange - she sets up the complaint but her husband controls the punchline
ultimately self-aware and willing to laugh at their shared aging quirks once she 'gets' the joke
emotional_range: wistful/resigned sadness (opening line, gaze drifted up and away from husband)
startled surprise ('What?', eyebrows up, head snapping toward him)
amused/knowing acknowledgment by the final beat, mouth curling into a small smirk
expressions: 0:00-0:03 - downcast, distant gaze toward the ceiling/window while delivering the complaint, corners of mouth turned down
0:03 - brief neutral pause after his 'We do', hands tighten slightly in her lap
0:04 - eyebrows shoot up, mouth opens on 'What?', head turns fully toward him for the first time
0:05-0:06 - eyes narrow into a knowing, faintly amused look as he says 'Acid reflex', small closed-mouth smirk
gestures: seated on the edge of the bed the entire scene, torso static, only the head/eyes move to track him
hands clasped together / fingers laced in her lap throughout - visible tension/self-soothing
slight forward lean and head-turn at 'What?' signaling she is actually listening now
characters.interactions_notes: She stays physically rooted on the bed while he moves and folds laundry across the room; the spatial distance between them visually underlines her opening complaint about having nothing in common. She does not look directly at him while making the complaint (gaze up/away), only turning to make eye contact once he answers - a small but telling avoidance beat. He holds the comedic power (delivers the punchline while continuing an unrelated chore), and she functions as the straight-man/reactor whose surprised 'What?' cues the joke's turn.

characters.name_or_role: husband (claymation man, glasses, hooked nose, black coat)
personality_traits: unbothered and low-key in the face of an emotionally loaded statement - keeps folding laundry without breaking stride
deadpan comic timing, delivers the punchline as a casual aside rather than a big reaction
domestically occupied/task-focused, treats a heart-to-heart as background noise to chores
quietly affectionate/wry - counters her pessimism with a joke instead of an argument
emotional_range: calm neutrality while she vents (no visible alarm or defensiveness)
sly, self-satisfied amusement building into a full grin on the 'Acid reflex' punchline
expressions: 0:00-0:03 - flat, focused expression aimed down at the clothes he is folding, not looking at her
0:03 - small, calm half-smile as he answers 'We do', still facing the chair/dresser
0:04-0:05 - smile widens slightly, faint smirk building as she reacts with 'What?'
0:05-0:06 - broad, toothy grin on 'Acid reflex', clearly pleased with his own line
gestures: stands and moves between the dresser/coat rack and the chair, methodically folding and setting down a stack of clothes/blankets
never stops the folding task while speaking - domestic chore continues uninterrupted through both his lines
body angled away from her for most of the exchange, only the head/eyes drift toward her as the punchline lands
characters.interactions_notes: He is the physically active character (crossing the room, handling laundry) while she remains static on the bed, creating a visual contrast between his routine-driven calm and her stationary emotional weight. He answers her without fully turning to face her, reinforcing the 'going through the motions' vibe implied by the episode title 'Burp-ees' and the show's 'Low Battery People' theme (a phone charges beside her throughout, echoing the idea of a relationship running on low power). The comedic power dynamic favors him - he gets the last word and the visual punch-in (grin) - while she supplies the emotional premise and the reaction that lands the joke.
